title: DOJ Files Record 88 Denaturalization Cases, Two Indian-Origin Citizens Targeted
excerpt: The Trump administration's largest coordinated citizenship revocation effort targets naturalized citizens from 17 countries, including an Indian-born H-1B fraudster and an investment scheme orchestrator.
body:
• The DOJ filed denaturalization complaints against 24 individuals between July 20 and August 3, bringing the total to 88 cases since January 2025.
  • Indian-origin citizens Neeraj Sharma and Debashis Ghosh are among those targeted — Sharma for H-1B visa fraud, Ghosh for a $2.5 million investment scheme.
  • The campaign spans 17 countries and covers offences from attempted murder to identity fraud, with officials calling it the largest coordinated effort in DOJ history.
  • Legal experts warn that naturalized citizens who concealed criminal histories or misrepresented facts during the citizenship process face growing scrutiny.

DOJ Announces Record Citizenship Revocation Push

The U.S. Department of Justice has filed denaturalization complaints against 24 naturalized citizens in what officials describe as the largest coordinated citizenship revocation effort in the department's history. The complaints, filed between July 20 and August 3, bring the administration's total denaturalization filings to 88 since President Trump took office in January 2025.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=jWonbek_PCI

"Today's filings represent the largest coordinated denaturalization effort in Department history, but they are only the beginning," Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said. The cases target citizens from 17 countries, including India, Pakistan, Mexico, Nigeria, Colombia, and Cuba.

Allegations range from attempted murder and child sexual abuse to identity fraud, marriage fraud, and practicing medicine without a licence. In each case, the government argues the individual obtained citizenship through fraud, concealment of criminal conduct, or willful misrepresentation during the naturalization process.

Two Indian-Origin Citizens in the Crosshairs

Among the individuals facing proceedings are two Indian-origin naturalized citizens whose cases illustrate the breadth of the campaign.

https://x.com/foxnewspolitics/status/2084374305241264265

Neeraj Sharma, a 50-year-old native of India and former CEO of New Jersey-based staffing company Magnavision LLC, is accused of filing 11 fraudulent H-1B visa petitions with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Each petition allegedly contained false representations that visa beneficiaries would be employed at a major global financial institution, complete with forged signatures on corporate letterhead. Sharma naturalized in 2017 after falsely asserting under penalty of perjury that he had never committed a crime or provided false information to government officials, according to the DOJ complaint.

Debashis Ghosh, 62, who entered the United States in the early 1990s on non-immigrant visas and naturalized in 2012, faces allegations of orchestrating a $2.5 million investment fraud. Federal officials say Ghosh conspired to defraud investors of funds meant for constructing an aircraft maintenance facility, continuing the scheme even after obtaining citizenship. During his naturalization interview, he stated he had never committed a crime for which he had not been arrested.

"Every one of these individuals committed crimes incompatible with U.S. citizenship. We are moving at record speed to denaturalize those who sought to deceive the federal government."

— Brett Shumate, Assistant Attorney General, DOJ Civil Division

A Broader Pattern of Enforcement

The latest batch follows a June round that targeted 17 individuals from 13 countries over allegations of child sexual abuse, narcotics trafficking, and large-scale financial fraud. In a separate batch announced in May, 12 individuals were charged, including cases involving support for terrorist organizations and war crimes.

Other cases in the latest filing include a Pakistani-origin citizen who filed multiple immigration applications under different aliases until obtaining permanent residency and citizenship under a false identity, and a Mexican-origin former priest convicted of stealing parish funds and secretly recording a minor.

The government's strategy relies on the Immigration and Nationality Act, which permits revocation of citizenship if naturalization was "illegally procured or procured by concealment of a material fact or by willful misrepresentation." If citizenship is revoked, individuals revert to their prior immigration status and may face deportation.

What It Means for Naturalized Citizens

The accelerating pace of denaturalization filings has unsettled immigrant communities, particularly those from South Asia. The DOJ has signalled it plans to file between 100 and 200 denaturalization referrals per month through fiscal year 2026, a dramatic escalation from historical norms where such cases were rare and typically limited to individuals who concealed involvement in genocide or Nazi-era crimes.

Legal advocates stress that the legal threshold for denaturalization remains high — the government must prove its case in federal court, and individuals retain full constitutional protections throughout the process. But the sheer volume of filings suggests a fundamental shift in how aggressively the government is scrutinizing naturalization records.

For the Indian diaspora, the cases of Sharma and Ghosh underscore a specific vulnerability: individuals who may have cut corners on visa applications or failed to disclose past legal issues now face a government apparatus actively mining historical records for discrepancies. Immigration attorneys recommend that naturalized citizens review their original applications and consult legal counsel if any information was omitted or misrepresented.

nri_angle: Two Indian-origin naturalized citizens face citizenship revocation — one for H-1B visa fraud, another for investment fraud — amid an unprecedented DOJ campaign that has rattled immigrant communities.
